title: The Sentence

learn.summary: The sentence is writing's unit of craft — everything larger is arrangement. Master three things: structure (how clauses combine), rhythm (how lengths vary), and control (how punctuation paces the reader). Gary Provost's famous demonstration says it all: five short sentences in a row deaden the ear; vary the lengths and 'the writing sings'.

do: Take one paragraph you wrote and count the words in each sentence; if the counts barely vary, rewrite for deliberate contrast.

children.title: Sentence Structures

learn.summary: English builds four structures from clauses: simple (one independent clause), compound (two joined by and/but/so), complex (independent plus dependent), compound-complex. Skilled writers also control where the main point lands — periodic sentences hold it until the end for suspense; loose sentences state it first, then elaborate. Knowing the names matters less than being able to build each on demand.

do: Write the same fact four ways — simple, compound, complex, and with the key point held to the final word — and pick the best.

children.title: Rhythm & Variety

learn.summary: Prose rhythm comes from varying sentence length and opening structure: a string of 20-word sentences hypnotizes, a string of 5-word ones hectors. The power move is contrast — a long, accumulating sentence followed by a short one. That lands. Parallelism is rhythm's other engine: matching grammatical forms for matching ideas ('of the people, by the people, for the people').

do: End one paragraph this week with a sentence of five words or fewer, placed after your longest sentence.

children.title: Punctuation as Control

learn.summary: Punctuation is stage direction: the period is a full stop, the semicolon yokes two related thoughts, the colon announces, the dash interrupts, parentheses whisper. The semicolon and dash are the underused pair — a semicolon shows two sentences are really one idea; a dash adds drama a comma cannot. Learn the comma splice (two sentences fused with only a comma) as the error editors catch first.

do: Write six sentences about your day using, correctly and deliberately: a semicolon, a colon, a pair of dashes, parentheses, a comma splice fixed two ways.

children.title: Common Errors

learn.summary: Four errors account for most red ink: comma splices, sentence fragments (fine in fiction, risky in reports), dangling modifiers ('Walking to work, the rain soaked me' — the rain was not walking), and agreement slips across long noun phrases. Strunk & White's Elementary Rules cover most of these in a few pages. Errors matter less for 'correctness' than for trust: readers who spot them start doubting your facts too.

do: Proofread your last substantial email for these four errors specifically, and keep a personal list of which ones you actually make.
